strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical derivation (Proposition 4.1) of an exact closed-form solution to the diffusion Stratonovich SDE via exponential integrators and the Dubins-Schwarz representation theorem, which is a technically sound and reasonably novel result.

The core motivation is well articulated: existing SDE inversion approaches (e.g., Wu & De la Torre, 2022) require storing the entire realized Wiener process, whereas the proposed method leverages Brownian intervals to achieve algebraic reversibility without this memory overhead, addressing a genuine practical limitation.

The related work section is thorough and clearly situates the contribution relative to ODE-based reversible solvers (EDICT, BELM, bidirectional integration approximation) and prior SDE inversion work, correctly identifying the key differentiator (memory efficiency).

The construction cleverly adapts the coupling-parameter idea from McCallum & Foster (2024), originally for neural ODEs, to the stochastic setting, which is a nontrivial extension requiring care with the Stratonovich integral and time-changed Brownian bridges.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is extremely thin: only a single qualitative figure (one image interpolation example) is presented, with no quantitative metrics (e.g., reconstruction error/PSNR to verify 'exact' inversion, FID/LPIPS for interpolation quality, or memory/runtime benchmarks) to substantiate the central claims.

The purported key advantage over Wu & De la Torre (2022) — memory savings from not storing the full Wiener process — is never empirically measured or compared (no memory footprint numbers, no wall-clock comparisons).

No ablations are provided on the coupling parameter ζ, the order of the truncated Stratonovich-Taylor expansion, or the number of discretization steps, so it is unclear how sensitive the method is to these choices or how it scales.

The experiment uses only one model (a single LDM on CelebA-HQ) and one task (face interpolation with 20 steps), which is insufficient to establish generality or significance across modalities/tasks mentioned in the introduction (e.g., audio, video, protein generation).

The authors explicitly frame the work as 'preliminary' with only 'proof of concept' experiments, and the promised application to continuous adjoint equations/guided generation—the other major motivating use case—is left entirely for future work, weakening the paper's demonstrated significance.

No direct experimental comparison is made against the most relevant baseline, Wu & De la Torre's SDE inversion method, despite it being discussed at length in related work; the only comparisons are to plain DDIM and McCallum-Foster's ODE-only reversible scheme.

The presentation of the core theoretical proposition and forward/backward pass equations is dense and notation-heavy, making it difficult to verify correctness without significant effort, and would benefit from more intuition or a simplified special case.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem: exact, memory-efficient inversion of diffusion SDEs, which is relevant for image editing, interpolation, and adjoint-based guided generation.

The theoretical derivation in Proposition 4.1 is a nontrivial piece of stochastic analysis, combining exponential integrators, a switch from Ito to Stratonovich integration, and the Dubins-Schwarz theorem to express the exact SDE solution as a linear term, an approximable drift integral, and a time-changed Brownian bridge that can be computed via the Brownian interval without storing the full Wiener path.
The construction cleverly adapts the coupling-parameter idea of McCallum & Foster (2024) from ODEs to the SDE setting, yielding an algebraically invertible discrete update (Eqs. 4.3-4.4).

The related work discussion appropriately situates the contribution relative to existing exact-inversion methods for diffusion ODEs (EDICT, BELM, bidirectional integration approximation) and the closest SDE-inversion baseline (Wu & De la Torre, 2022), clarifying the claimed memory advantage.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is essentially a single qualitative figure (one pair of faces, one interpolation sequence) with no quantitative metrics (e.g., reconstruction error/PSNR/LPIPS, FID for generation quality, or wall-clock/memory measurements) to substantiate the central claims of exact inversion, improved stability, or memory efficiency.

The two motivating issues raised in Section 3 (truncation-error mismatch and numerical stability) are never empirically or theoretically quantified for the proposed solver; the paper explicitly defers 'a more detailed analysis of stability' to future work, leaving the core motivation unaddressed.

The application to continuous adjoint equations / guided generation, prominently mentioned in the abstract and motivation as a key use case, is not demonstrated at all; it is left entirely as future work, weakening the significance claim.

No comparison against the closest existing SDE-inversion baseline (Wu & De la Torre, 2022) or other SDE solvers (e.g., SEEDS) is provided, despite explicit textual comparison in the related work; the paper only compares against DDIM (an ODE solver) and its own reversible variant.

Key implementation choices (order of the Stratonovich-Taylor truncation used for Ψh, choice of ζ=0.999 and its sensitivity, number of Brownian interval subdivisions, computational/memory overhead of the Brownian interval in practice) are not ablated or justified quantitatively.

The theory assumes the data-prediction model is trained to zero loss (x̂0|t = x0|t), which never holds in practice; the paper does not analyze or empirically assess how model approximation error affects the exactness/reversibility guarantees that are central to the paper's claims.

Reproducibility is weak: no code is released or promised, and Appendix C provides only minimal experimental details (hardware, dataset, pretrained model URL) without hyperparameters, solver order, or sufficient detail to reproduce Figure 1.

The contribution is largely a combination of existing techniques (McCallum & Foster's coupling-parameter reversibility, Kidger et al.'s Brownian interval, standard exponential-integrator/Stratonovich machinery for diffusion SDEs) applied to a new setting, which is a reasonable but incremental novelty given the lack of strong empirical validation.

The paper self-describes as 'preliminary work' and 'proof of concept' in the limitations, which combined with the lack of quantitative results indicates the work is not yet mature enough for publication at a top venue.

strengths: The paper derives a genuinely interesting closed-form/exponential-integrator expression for the exact solution of the diffusion reverse-time SDE (Proposition 4.1), decomposing it into a linear term, an approximated drift term, and a time-changed Brownian bridge term, with a careful proof using the Fisk-Stratonovich integral and the Dubins-Schwarz representation theorem.

The motivation section (Section 3) clearly articulates two concrete, well-known problems with naive forward/backward solving of diffusion ODEs/SDEs (truncation-error mismatch and numerical instability), which is a good, well-argued setup for the proposed contribution.

The idea of combining the McCallum & Foster (2024) coupling-parameter construction for algebraically reversible solvers with the diffusion SDE's exponential-integrator formulation, together with the Brownian interval (Kidger et al., 2021) to avoid storing the full Wiener path, is a reasonably novel combination that plausibly addresses a real memory bottleneck in prior exact-inversion-for-SDE work (e.g., Wu & De la Torre, 2022).

Related work coverage is fairly thorough, situating the contribution among ODE-based exact inversion methods (EDICT, BDIA, BELM) and prior SDE inversion approaches, with a clear technical distinction drawn against Wu & De la Torre (2022).
weaknesses: Experimental validation is extremely thin: the entire empirical evaluation consists of a single qualitative interpolation example on one image pair from one dataset (CelebA-HQ) with one pretrained LDM. There are no quantitative metrics (e.g., reconstruction PSNR/LPIPS, FID for interpolations, or numerical inversion error) and no results across multiple samples or seeds, making it impossible to assess robustness or general applicability of the claims.

The central claimed advantage of the method — exact inversion without storing the full Wiener process in memory — is never empirically substantiated. No memory usage or runtime comparison is given against the natural baseline (Wu & De la Torre, 2022) that does store the full noise realization, so the paper's main practical selling point is asserted but not demonstrated.

No comparison to the closest prior SDE-inversion baseline (Wu & De la Torre, 2022) is included in experiments, only to ODE-based DDIM and its McCallum-Foster reversible variant; this omission weakens the evidentiary support for superiority or even parity of the proposed approach.

Stability of the constructed solver, which is heavily motivated in Section 3 as a key desideratum, is not formally analyzed for the proposed scheme (e.g., region of convergence as a function of the coupling parameter ζ); the paper only qualitatively notes better visual stability in one example, and explicitly defers a "detailed analysis of stability" to future work.

The exactness claims in the abstract/title ("exact inversion," "algebraically reversible") should be more carefully qualified: only the linear and Brownian-bridge terms are exact, while the drift/approximated term still carries truncation error, so the guarantee is really forward-backward algebraic consistency rather than zero approximation error relative to the true SDE solution; this distinction is somewhat glossed over in the framing.

The paper is very short (4 pages of main content) with a single small-scale proof-of-concept experiment, and the authors themselves label the work "preliminary," which, combined with the lack of quantitative results, ablations (e.g., varying ζ, step counts, higher-order truncations), and additional modalities/datasets despite motivating the work with audio, video, and protein generation, limits the paper's demonstrated significance for the main research track.

strengths: The paper makes a genuinely elegant theoretical contribution, connecting the neural-ODE reversible-solver literature (McCallum-Foster) with the exponential-integrator/Lawson-method literature for diffusion models, yielding a unified construction (Rex) applicable to both the probability-flow ODE and the reverse-time SDE.

Rigorous convergence theory is provided: Theorem 4.1 shows Rex inherits the order of the underlying explicit RK scheme for the ODE case, and Theorem 4.2 shows the analogous strong-order result for the SDE case, both with detailed proofs in the appendix.

The paper claims (and provides supporting derivation for) the first algebraically reversible SDE solver for diffusion models that avoids storing the full Brownian motion trajectory, addressing a genuine practical memory bottleneck, by leveraging splittable PRNG-based Brownian motion reconstruction.

Extensive appendix (Theorem E.1 and many propositions) shows Rex subsumes numerous well-known existing samplers (DDIM, DPM-Solver family, SDE-DPM-Solver, SEEDS-1, gDDIM) as special/non-reversible cases, which is a compelling unifying result strengthening the significance of the framework.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across unconditional (DDPM/CelebA-HQ) and conditional (Stable Diffusion v1.5/COCO) settings with several relevant reversible baselines (EDICT, BDIA, O-BELM) and standard metrics (FID, CLIP score, ImageReward).

Commendable transparency about limitations: the paper explicitly reports failure cases (e.g., Appendix J/K show Rex(ShARK) with data-prediction diverging/overflowing, and non-Gaussian, artifact-laden latents under some settings) rather than hiding them.

A clear taxonomy/comparison table (Table 3) situates Rex against prior reversible solvers along axes of extra memory, truncation error, stability, and existence of convergence proofs, clarifying the paper's contribution relative to existing work.
weaknesses: The presentation is very dense and notation-heavy, with the core algorithmic contribution split across many propositions/lemmas/appendices; a reader cannot easily extract a simple, implementable algorithm description from the main text alone, hurting accessibility.

Empirical validation is comparatively narrow: only one unconditional model/dataset (DDPM on CelebA-HQ) and one conditional model (SD v1.5 on COCO captions) are tested; no evaluation on other modalities or model families (e.g., flow-matching models, larger-scale or video diffusion) despite claims of broad applicability.

No wall-clock time, memory, or NFE-normalized efficiency comparisons are reported, even though Rex requires extra state, exponential-map evaluations, and (for SDE) space-time Lévy-area terms; the practical cost/benefit trade-off versus simpler or non-reversible solvers is left unquantified.

The results are somewhat mixed rather than uniformly favorable: e.g., in Table 1, O-BELM outperforms Rex(RK4) in FID at 10 and 20 steps; in Table 2, Rex(Midpoint) narrowly beats others at 50 steps but Rex is not uniformly dominant across step counts and metrics, which is not fully reflected in the more favorable narrative tone of Section 5.

Stability and robustness to the coupling hyperparameter ζ is under-explored empirically; Appendix J shows extreme sensitivity (variance blowing up ~10^7) and failure cases depending on parameterization (data vs. noise prediction) and underlying scheme (e.g., ShARK), suggesting practical brittleness that is not thoroughly characterized or mitigated.

Comparisons are restricted to other reversible/exact-inversion solvers; no comparison against strong non-reversible fast samplers (e.g., DPM-Solver++, UniPC) is given to contextualize how much sample-quality cost reversibility imposes relative to state-of-the-art non-reversible sampling.

Quantitative experiments use a single fixed seed and relatively modest sample counts (10,240 unconditional samples, 1,000 captions), with no reported variance/error bars across seeds, limiting confidence in the statistical robustness of the comparisons.

The ethics statement is minimal (a single sentence) given that the work is presented as directly relevant to diffusion-based image editing/inversion pipelines, which have documented misuse potential (e.g., face manipulation), and could benefit from more substantive discussion.

strengths: Elegant theoretical framework connecting the McCallum-Foster reversible-solver construction with Lawson/exponential integrator methods, yielding a unified family (Rex) of reversible solvers for both the probability-flow ODE and reverse-time SDE.

Strong theoretical results: Theorem 4.1 shows Rex inherits arbitrarily high convergence order in the ODE case, and Theorem 4.2 shows it preserves the strong convergence order of the underlying SRK scheme in the SDE case, with full proofs provided in the appendix.

Extensive appendix (Appendix E) rigorously shows that Rex subsumes many well-known diffusion solvers (DDIM, DPM-Solver-1/2/++1/++(2S)/12, SDE-DPM-Solver variants, SEEDS-1, gDDIM) as special/underlying cases, giving the framework good explanatory and unifying value.

To the authors' knowledge, the first algebraically reversible SDE solver for diffusion models that does not require storing the entire Brownian path trajectory in memory, a genuine practical advance over CycleDiffusion-style approaches.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across unconditional (CelebA-HQ, DDPM) and conditional (Stable Diffusion v1.5, COCO prompts) generation, plus an interpolation case study, with honest reporting of failure cases (e.g., ShARK data-prediction overflow, Figure 9).

Good positioning relative to prior reversible solvers (EDICT, BDIA, BELM, asynchronous leapfrog, reversible Heun) with explicit stability/convergence-order comparisons (Table 3), including proofs that BDIA and O-BELM are nowhere linearly stable.
weaknesses: Empirical superiority of Rex is inconsistent: in Table 1, Rex (RK4) is often worse than O-BELM (e.g., FID 31.00 vs 27.26 at 10 steps, 23.49 vs 20.15 at 20 steps), and only Rex (Euler-Maruyama) at 50 steps clearly wins; the paper does not adequately reconcile these mixed results with the claimed advantages of the method.

The interpolation experiment (Figure 5) shows that the deterministic ODE variants of Rex fail to interpolate smoothly, undermining the generality of the proposed reversible framework and suggesting the stochastic variant's success may be case-specific.

Appendix J documents genuine failure modes (variance blow-up to ~10^7 for data-prediction Rex-Euler, ShARK overflow errors for data prediction) which raise concerns about the practical robustness and hyperparameter sensitivity (choice of zeta, parameterization) of the proposed solvers.

Despite one of the three headline goals being improved stability, the achieved region of stability is only 'non-trivial' and still smaller than that of the underlying RK scheme (Theorem A.2); the stability improvement over prior reversible solvers, while real, is modest and not quantitatively benchmarked against non-reversible baselines.

Experiments are limited to a single unconditional model/dataset (DDPM/CelebA-HQ) and a single conditional model (SD v1.5/COCO); despite the introduction citing video, protein, and biometric applications, no experiments beyond image diffusion are provided, limiting evidence for broader significance.

No computational cost or wall-clock comparison is provided, despite the added complexity of exponential/Lawson reparameterizations and stochastic Levy-area terms (ShARK), leaving efficiency trade-offs of Rex versus simpler baselines unaddressed.

The presentation is extremely notation-heavy and dependent on a 61-page appendix for essentially all derivations and many implementation details (e.g., closed-form inverse noise-schedule functions), which may hinder reproducibility and accessibility for readers relying only on the 9-page main text.
The ethics statement is a single generic sentence and does not meaningfully engage with potential misuse in image editing/inversion pipelines beyond acknowledgment.
